title: Weight-Loss Drugs Just Showed They May Cut Cancer Risk by Up to 71 Per Cent. South Asians Should Be Paying Close Attention.
excerpt: Six studies presented at ASCO 2026 found GLP-1 medications linked to dramatically lower rates of pancreatic, lung, breast, and blood cancers. The implications for a community with among the world's highest diabetes rates are enormous.
body:
The drugs that were supposed to treat diabetes and help people lose weight may also be fighting cancer. That is the headline from this year's American Society of Clinical Oncology annual meeting in Chicago, where six separate studies presented evidence that GLP-1 medications — the class that includes Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound — are associated with significantly lower cancer risk across multiple tumour types.

The numbers are striking. A study of 572,000 people at high risk of pancreatic cancer, conducted by Jefferson Einstein Hospital in Philadelphia, found that cases were 71 per cent lower among those using GLP-1 drugs. A University of Pennsylvania analysis of more than 110,000 women found GLP-1 users were roughly 30 per cent less likely to develop breast cancer. A Cleveland Clinic study of 12,000 type 2 diabetes patients found those on GLP-1 injections were up to 50 per cent less likely to see their lung, liver, bowel, or breast cancer progress to stage four.

## What the Science Says

The findings span half a dozen studies and cover an unusually wide range of cancer types. A Jefferson Einstein study of 68,000 people at high risk of lung cancer found a 31 per cent reduction in diagnoses among GLP-1 users. Researchers at the universities of Indiana and Florida found that users were up to 30 per cent less likely to develop blood cancers like leukaemia. And a seven-year study with nearly 120,000 participants found GLP-1s were associated with lower rates of new prostate cancer diagnoses.

"These drugs have never been just glucose-lowering agents," said Dr Marcin Chwistek of the Fox Chase Cancer Center in Philadelphia at an ASCO press briefing. "What's new here is the consistency across tumour types, and data this large and this consistent warrant a prospective randomised trial."

The mechanisms are not fully understood. Weight loss alone does not explain the results. Researchers at the University of Texas San Antonio reported that GLP-1 users in their prostate cancer study had only a "very small" reduction in body weight at one year, yet still showed lower cancer rates. The hypothesis now centres on the drugs' anti-inflammatory and immune-modulating properties, which may independently suppress tumour growth.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

South Asians have among the highest rates of type 2 diabetes in the world. Studies consistently show that Indians develop diabetes a decade earlier than their Western counterparts and at lower body weights. This means a disproportionate number of South Asians are already on GLP-1 medications or are candidates for them.

The cancer angle adds a new dimension to an existing conversation. If you are an NRI managing diabetes with Ozempic or Mounjaro, these findings suggest your medication may be doing more than controlling blood sugar. If your parents in India are on metformin and considering newer options, the cancer data becomes another factor in that discussion.

Pancreatic cancer, which showed the most dramatic risk reduction at 71 per cent, is also disproportionately aggressive in South Asian populations. Breast cancer incidence among Indian women has been rising sharply. The GLP-1 data, while not yet proven through randomised trials, offers a rare piece of genuinely hopeful news.

## The Important Caveats

Nearly all of the data presented at ASCO were from observational studies, not randomised controlled trials. Patients prescribed GLP-1 drugs may differ from comparison groups in ways that influence outcomes — better access to healthcare, different lifestyle patterns, concurrent treatments.

"I think there is enough data to show there is clearly some impact on modulation of cancer — either the cancer risk or the risk of recurrence — but we haven't yet defined exactly what that signal is or that benefit is," said Eleonora Teplinsky, ASCO's breast cancer expert. She cautioned against taking GLP-1 drugs solely to reduce cancer risk at this stage.

Prospective randomised trials are now being planned. Penn Medicine is actively working to set up a multisite clinical trial to assess whether GLP-1 medications can lower breast cancer incidence among high-risk women. Until those results arrive, these findings are a signal, not a prescription.

## What Comes Next

The pharmaceutical implications are significant. If GLP-1 drugs can be shown to prevent or slow cancer in controlled trials, the already enormous market — Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly generated tens of billions from these medications in 2025 — could expand dramatically. For NRI investors holding pharma positions, this is worth tracking.

For the diaspora community, the practical takeaway is straightforward. If you or your family are managing diabetes or obesity, discuss GLP-1 options with your physician. The primary benefits in blood sugar control and weight management are well established. The potential cancer protection, while unproven, adds weight to a conversation many South Asian families need to have but keep putting off.
